newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Credit Suisse fund attracts Russian mattress money.
newsitem.headline: Credit Suisse fund attracts Russian mattress money.

text.p: Russians have already pulled 28 billion roubles ($5 million) from under their mattresses and bank accounts to buy into Credit Suisse's recently-launched domestic mutual funds, the Swiss banking group said on Thursday.
Credit Suisse Investment Funds (Moscow), a Credit Suisse Group unit, has two fixed income funds and will launch a third on January 31 that will invest in large-capitalisation Russian shares.

The first fund, which concentrates on rouble-denominated fixed-income instruments such as treasury bills, began on December 15, 1996. It has already attracted 28 billion roubles, said Nikolai Klekovkin, deputy chief executive officer of CS Investment Funds in Moscow.

Beatrice Hollond, Managing Director of Credit Suisse Asset Management and responsible for the funds' investment strategy, said the T-bill fund could offer exceptional returns, but the fixed income approach would be relatively conservative.
She said T-bill yields could rise five to 10 percent on political uncertainty, although she said the overall trend was towards lower yields as Russian stability increased.
Yields have dropped recently to just above 30 percent from nearly 40 percent two months ago.
Credit Suisse said it saw Russian gross domestic product rising one percent this year and three percent in 1998 with inflation of 17 and 12 percent respectively.
Hollond said the funds would have to maintain high liquidity, especially as they are being introduced to sceptical Russians who hold up to $30 billion in cash as savings.
"People may put their money in and test it," she said, adding that new clients might invest and withdraw a number of times to try liquidity.
Klekovkin said the first fund had two major institutional investors, in addition to average investors who each put in about $500-$2,000.
"Probably 20 percent of our target group knows what a unit fund is," he said.
Four unit fund groups in Russia have begun collecting money including Credit Suisse, Pallada Asset Management, Pioneer First Fund managed by KUIF and Troika-Dialog Asset Management.
Pallada Asset Management announced on Wednesday it had reached 2.6 billion roubles investment, which would allow it to begin investing funds.
